title: Wetlands! Wetlands! Wetlands!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore wetlands: what defines them (periodic or permanent saturation, hydric soil, anaerobic conditions, hydrophytic plants), the main types (tidal and freshwater marshes, mangrove forests, inland swamps including the Okefinokee, bogs and fens, prairie potholes, playas, vernal pools/ephemeral wetlands, seeps, oxbow lakes/billabongs), how plants adapt to waterlogged soil (cattail aerenchyma, speckled alder lenticels, salt-excreting cordgrass, bald cypress knees, carnivorous plants), the history of US wetland loss and the Clean Water Act, and why wetlands matter (flood storage, water filtration, habitat for fish and birds, beaver dams). The episode closes with listener mail about the Stuff You Should Know virtual 5K.
topics: wetland loss in the United States

segments.title: Book plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts plug their book, an Incomplete Compendium of mostly Interesting Things, then open the episode with banter about wetlands and a shout-out to biologist Tom Peterman.

segments.title: Defining wetlands and US wetland loss
segments.summary: Wetlands are defined by periodic or permanent saturation, hydric soil and anaerobic conditions. Wetlands cover about 5 percent of US land, and the US has drained them heavily, with about 220 million acres in the Lower 48 in the 1600s and losses continuing into the mid-20th century until the Clean Water Act.

segments.title: Coastal wetlands: marshes, tidal marshes and mangroves
segments.summary: Coastal marshes sit between inland areas and the ocean and are often brackish. Salt marshes are dominated by grasses, freshwater tidal marshes are affected by tides but not salt, and the Great Lakes also have tides. Mangrove forests have roots standing out of the water and provide habitat and shoreline benefits.

segments.title: Inland wetlands: swamps, ephemeral wetlands, vernal pools and prairie potholes
segments.summary: Inland wetlands include swamps, marshes and bogs near rivers and streams. Many are ephemeral and dry for much of the year. Vernal pools serve as nurseries for amphibians, prairie potholes left by glaciers serve migratory birds, and playa lakes in deserts also attract migrating birds.

segments.title: Inland swamps and the Okefinokee
segments.summary: Hosts describe a canoe camping trip in the Okefinokee Swamp, with reserved raised platforms, alligators and no shade. They explain that the Okefinokee is a non-riverine swamp forest fed by rain or groundwater, while bottomland hardwood swamps are river fed and typically have shrub swamp buffers.

segments.title: Bogs, fens and bog bodies
segments.summary: Bogs are highly acidic, nutrient-poor, anaerobic peat wetlands, while fens are fed by groundwater and are more nutrient-rich and diverse. Bog bodies are preserved because of acidity and anaerobic conditions that slow decomposition.

segments.title: Other wetlands: seeps, creeks, oxbow lakes and billabongs
segments.summary: Other wetland types include mud flats, seeps where springs spill over the ground, and creeks. An oxbow lake forms when a river meanders away, and in Australia the Aboriginal name for it is billabong.

segments.title: How plants adapt to waterlogged soil
segments.summary: Wetland hydrologists study how water moves into and out of wetlands. Because waterlogged soil lacks oxygen, wetland plants adapt: cattails move oxygen from leaves to roots, speckled alders have lenticels, salt marsh grasses excrete salt, bald cypress grow knees for oxygen, and carnivorous plants get nutrients from insects.

segments.title: Why wetlands matter and how to help
segments.summary: Wetlands store floodwater, filter pollution, provide habitat for fish, birds and wildlife, and are sometimes called the kidneys of the earth. Beaver dams create similar wetlands. Hosts mention conservation groups, note that much wetland is privately owned, describe local buffer rules in Atlanta, and urge voting for local officials who protect wetlands.

segments.title: Listener mail: virtual 5K
segments.summary: A listener reports on the Stuff You Should Know virtual 5K, where participants ran or walked while listening to episodes and shared photos, and the organizer says the event built community.
